bio.en: Jenny Wen leads design for Claude Cowork at Anthropic, and was previously director of design at Figma (leading the FigJam and Slides teams) and a designer at Dropbox, Square, and Shopify; she offers a glimpse of where the design profession is heading.
bio.zh: Jenny Wen 在 Anthropic 领导 Claude Cowork 的设计，此前是 Figma 的设计总监（领导 FigJam 和 Slides 团队），并在 Dropbox、Square 和 Shopify 担任设计师；她向我们展示了设计职业正走向何方。

summary.en: Jenny argues the old design-process gospel is dead: with AI, designers no longer have time to make beautiful mocks (prototyping has dropped from 60–70% to 30–40% of the role), and the job is now helping engineers and teams execute. Design visions have compressed from multi-year decks to three-to-six-month prototypes, and even engineers struggle to keep up with their own agents. She shares what she now looks for when hiring (three emerging designer archetypes) and where human judgment, taste, and accountability still matter most. It's a wild, practical look at the near future of design.
summary.zh: Jenny 主张旧的设计流程“圣经”已死：在 AI 时代，设计师不再有时间为每个方案做精美 mock（原型工作从占角色的 60%–70% 降到 30%–40%），工作变成了帮助工程师和团队去执行。设计愿景也从多年期的精美 deck 压缩成三到六个月的原型，连工程师都难以跟上自己那一堆智能体的节奏。她分享了如今招聘设计师时看重的点（三种新兴设计师画像），以及人类的判断、品味与责任在哪里依然最关键。这期节目是对设计近未来一次大胆又务实的窥探。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: This design process that designers have been taught, we sort of treat it as gospel. That's basically dead. You as a designer actually do not have the time to make these beautiful mocks anymore.
turns.zh: 设计师们一直以来所接受的这种设计流程，我们几乎把它奉为圭臬。但如今这种流程已经行不通了。作为设计师，你根本没有时间再去制作那些精美的模型了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A big part of the design role now is helping engineers and teams execute, not just telling them, "Here's the design."
turns.zh: 如今设计师角色的很大一部分，是帮助工程师和团队执行任务，而不仅仅是告诉他们：“这就是设计方案。”

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: A few years ago, 60 to 70% of it was mocking and prototyping, but now I feel the mocking up part of it is 30 to 40%.
turns.zh: 几年前，有60%到70%的时间用于模型设计和原型制作，但现在我觉得模型设计环节只占30%到40%的时间了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're better off not blocking that, letting them cook.
turns.zh: 你最好别去阻拦他们，让他们自由发挥。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: It's not just designers who are feeling like, "Oh yeah, we have to keep up with engineers." I think even engineers are like, "How do we keep up with ourselves?"
turns.zh: 不只是设计师们在感叹“天啊，我们得跟上工程师的节奏了”。我觉得就连工程师们也在想：“我们要怎么跟上自己的节奏呢？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How to keep up with all our agents, our seven agents who are constantly running?
turns.zh: 要如何跟上我们所有代理的节奏？我们有七个代理，他们每天都在忙个不停。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: The result of engineering changing a bunch is that design is sort of forced to change. We used to go off and make this two-year, five-year, 10-year vision even. Now it becomes a vision that's three to six months out, and isn't necessarily creating this beautiful deck, sometimes just creating a prototype that points people in the right direction.
turns.zh: 工程部门的大量变革导致设计部门被迫随之调整。我们曾经会花两年，五年，甚至十年去构思愿景。现在愿景往往只需三到六个月就能确定，而且不一定需要制作精美的演示文稿，有时只需制作一个能为团队指明方向的原型就足够了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Boris on the podcast recently was saying Claude Code is now helping him come up with ideas.
turns.zh: 最近播客中的Boris提到，Claude Code现在正在帮助他构思创意。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: And we'll get better at taste and judgment and design. We might be holding onto that a little bit too much.
turns.zh: 我们需要不断提升审美品味和设计判断力。或许我们对这些方面的执着有些过头了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where will human brains continue to be valuable?
turns.zh: 未来人类的大脑在哪些领域仍将具有不可替代的价值？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: At the end of the day, someone has to decide what is actually going to get built and what actually matters. Someone still needs to be accountable for the decision.
turns.zh: 归根结底，总得有人来决定哪些方案会真正投入生产，哪些才是真正重要的。始终需要有人为这些决策负责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you now look for when you're hiring designers?
turns.zh: 现在招聘设计师时，你会看重哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: There's probably three archetypes of folks that are really interesting to me right now.
turns.zh: 目前有三种设计师原型让我觉得特别有趣。

turns.zh: 我一直很期待这次对话，因为我在播客中花了很多时间谈论软件工程的未来，讨论这个角色的转变，以及产品管理角色的变化。我甚至花了大量时间探讨设计领域的变革。显然，这些领域的变革也非常显著。而你正身处变革前沿，见证着事态的发展方向。我知道你对行业趋势有着深刻的见解，所以我有很多想聊的话题。首先，我想先抛出一个宏观问题：随着人工智能的兴起，设计流程将如何发生变化？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: It's changing a lot. I think it's still also got a long way to go in terms of the way it's changing. I think we've actually seen engineering change a lot more in the past little while than design actually has, but I think the result of engineering changing a bunch is that design is sort of forced to change. And so I think some context around this, is I did a talk at a conference in Berlin a few months ago in September, and I called it Don't Trust the Design Process, where I basically just said, "Hey, you know this design process that designers have been taught, where you go and you go off and you do a bunch of research and discovery, and then you diverge, you converge, diverge, converge." And it's like this process that we sort of treated as gospel and tried so hard to preserve and we were like, "Trust the process." That's basically dead. (00:05:52): I think it was sort of dying before the age of AI, but given now that engineers can go off and spin off their seven Claudes, I think as designers, we really have to let go of that process. And I think that's the big thing that's changing. But I think even in the past three to four months since I did that talk, that talk actually starts to feel pretty ... It kind of feels outdated to me, which is a little embarrassing, but especially with the big shift of Opus 46 and a bunch of folks just really discovering and using Claude Code over the holiday break, I think we're seeing this force to change our process happen even more. The way I see it now is there are basically two types of design work, and design work is becoming really stratified in this new world. (00:06:42): So there's the first one, which is really just supporting the implementation and execution. So this is the one where engineers are using their seven Claudes to create all these features, and anybody can put an idea out there, and you can just talk about an idea and somebody, usually actually an engineer because they're still better at implementing this stuff than we are, they will just make a scrappy version of it and you can try it out. And you as a designer actually do not have the time to make these beautiful mocks anymore, or to lead in this way. (00:07:16): And then I think there's the second kind of work that feels also really important, which is creating the sort of vision or direction for things. This one feels like the hardest to make time for, and it's one that we still did before, but I think the shape of it's very much changing, because I think we used to go off and say, "We're going to do this design vision. We're going to go off and make this two-year, five-year, whatever, 10-year vision even, and we're going to point us towards something." But the way that the technology is changing now, we don't know what's going to happen in two years. There's too much changing, and it usually becomes a vision that's three to six months out, and isn't necessarily something that is creating this beautiful deck that's beautifully story told. It's sometimes just creating a prototype that points people in the right direction. (00:08:06): And I think this kind of work is still really important in this world because in a world where people can spin off their seven Claudes, make whatever features they want in any kind of direction or in implementation, you need to point them towards something. And in order to make sure that we're all making something that makes sense together and is also done in a way where it's efficient. If we're all working towards something that has one greater cause, it's much more efficient to do that than just random things. (00:08:35): And so that's the big shift that I'm seeing. And I think I have opinions about it now, but ask me in three months and it might actually change even more.
turns.zh:
情况变化巨大。就其变化趋势而言，我认为仍有很长的路要走。过去这段时间里，工程领域的变革远比设计领域显著得多，但工程变革带来的结果是，设计不得不被迫随之调整。几个月前，我在柏林参加了一场会议，并在会上发表了题为《别迷信设计流程》的演讲。我在演讲中直言："大家都知道设计师常用的流程——先调研、发现问题，再分散探索、汇总结果、再分散探索、再汇总……"这种被奉为圭臬、被反复坚守的流程，如今已名存实亡。（00:05:52）：在人工智能时代到来之前，这种流程就已式微，而如今工程师们可以随意开发自己的"七个Claude"（注：Claude可能指某款AI工具），设计师们不得不彻底放下这种流程。这才是真正变革的核心。但即便在演讲后的三四个月里，这番论述也显得有些过时。这尤其体现在Opus 46的大爆发，以及节假日期间许多人突然发现并开始使用Claude Code上。变革的压力正与日俱增。在我看来，当下设计工作主要分为两类：（00:06:42）：第一类是支持工程实施与落地。这类工作中，工程师们用Claude快速开发功能，任何人都能提出想法，设计师只需参与讨论，工程师（毕竟他们在实现功能方面更专业）就能迅速制作出原型供测试。设计师已无暇顾及精美的模型或主导整个过程。（00:07:16）：第二类同样重要，但获取时间越来越难。这类工作曾是我们的专长，但如今形态已变。过去我们会制定两三年甚至十年的愿景，但如今技术变化太快，难以预测未来。愿景往往缩短至三到六个月，且不一定需要精美的PPT展示，更多是指导性的原型。（00:08:06）：这类工作在当下依然重要。在工程师可以随意开发Claude功能、任意方向落地的情况下，设计师必须为其指明方向。只有在全员朝着共同目标努力时，才能实现高效协作。
就是些零零碎碎的事儿。（00:08:35）：这就是我所看到的重大转变。我现在对此有一些看法，但三个月后再问我，也许观点会发生更大的变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what you're saying here is it's not like you or the design field is like, "We need to change?" It's engineering and the fact that you can build so quickly, just forces the role of a designer to change because as you said, engineers can just ship, ship, ship, ship, ship. And what you're finding here is you're better off not blocking that, letting them cook, as they say. And then there's this mode of helping them along as they ship, bring it together, make sure it all connects, guide them a little bit.
turns.zh: 你的意思是说，并不是你或者设计领域的人会觉得“我们需要改变”？而是工程领域的快速开发迫使设计师的角色发生了变化，正如你所说，工程师可以不断地“上线、上线、上线”。你发现的最佳策略是顺其自然，让他们专注于开发，然后在他们上线产品时提供协助，确保各部分衔接顺畅，并给予适当指导。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, I think so. Yeah. I don't think there is one unifying voice that's like, "Designers, we need to change right now." But yeah, there is the follow-on effects of engineering tooling really changing. I think we'll probably see design tooling change in this next year or so as well, but a lot of it right now is trailing that. And I think it's also really empowering for us too, because as designers, we also now have access to a lot of these coding tools. And we can be a part of the process in a way where we're implementing stuff. I'm doing a lot of last mile stuff where I'm implementing all the polish, and working with engineers really closely to get the feature across the line, and also prototype stuff in actual code as opposed to relying on engineers to do that again.
turns.zh: 是的，我也这么认为。是的，我不认为有哪个行业会统一呼吁“设计师们，我们现在就必须改变”。但工程开发工具的快速迭代确实带来了连锁反应。我认为未来一年左右，设计工具也会迎来变革，但目前很多工具仍在追赶趋势。这对我们设计师来说也意义重大，因为我们现在也能使用许多编程工具，参与到开发过程中。我现在负责最后的润色工作，与工程师密切合作，确保功能顺利上线，还能用实际代码制作原型，而不必依赖工程师来完成这些工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How true do you think this is at all companies, at say AI companies, non-AI companies? Someone may be hearing this, okay, Anthropic Claude, okay, they're at the bleeding edge, for one. Two, it's developery a little bit, but I think people might be feeling like, "Okay, this is not going to happen at Salesforce. This is not going to happen at, I don't know, ServiceNow, wherever." So I guess, do you feel like this is where all teams are heading? Is it mostly AI, bleeding edge companies? How widespread do you think the design process shift is going to be?
turns.zh: 你觉得这种情况在所有公司都适用吗？比如人工智能公司、非人工智能公司？有些人可能会听到这些观点，比如Anthropic的Claude，他们处于技术前沿。二来，开发者们也需要跟上进度。但人们可能觉得“好吧，这在Salesforce不会发生。在ServiceNow之类的公司更不会。”所以我想，你觉得所有团队都在朝着这个方向发展吗？主要是在人工智能领域、前沿科技公司吗？你认为设计流程的变革会普及到多大程度？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: So the talk that I did last year has really been the most resonant talk that I've done. And so I think it's something that people are starting to feel across the industry, where they're like, "Oh yeah, we can't do the old design process anymore. We are using tools like Claude Code and v0 and whatnot, to start to spin up prototypes, and PMs are starting to spin up prototypes and stuff like that as well." So I think there's something there emerging. But the other interesting observation with that talk too, was there was actually also a decent amount of backlash. People clearly have invested their entire careers in learning, teaching, using this really stable design process. And I think there was a lot of discrediting like, "Oh yeah, we can't do without discovery. We can't do without these pieces of process." So I think there is still a piece of the industry that is not quite there yet in terms of this way of working, if that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我去年做的演讲至今反响最热烈。我觉得整个行业都开始意识到这一点，人们会说“哦，是的，我们不能再用老旧的设计流程了。我们在用Claude Code、v0之类的工具快速制作原型，产品经理也开始这么做了。”所以我觉得确实有一些积极的变化。但那次演讲也有个有趣的现象，就是遭遇了不少抵制。人们显然把整个职业生涯都投入到学习、教学和使用这种稳定的设计流程中去了。我觉得仍有相当一部分行业从业者还没能完全适应这种工作方式，如果你能理解我的意思的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And a big part of this is you could argue ... the question is what leads to the best, most successful products in companies? And you could argue it's spending time doing discovery, user research, mocks, iterating, beta testing, or it could be just engineer shipper stuff that's okay, not amazing, good enough. We learn, iterate, build, iterate. Is your sense that that second path, not only is that just what everyone's doing, but that actually leads to the better product at this point?
turns.zh: 其中很重要的一点是，你可以争辩说……问题在于，什么能让公司的产品最出色、最成功？你可能会说，是花时间进行探索、用户研究、模型设计、迭代、Beta测试，或者只是做些工程师式的交付——这些都还不错，但并非惊艳之作，仅够用。我们不断学习、迭代、构建、再迭代。你是否认为第二种路径不仅是大家都在走的路，而且在当下确实能带来更优质的产品？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I think you sort of have to choose and use your discretion as to when to actually ship something, but I think the ability to execute, try something out and try it with real data, and a real user's kind of mindset in the product, I think that does lead to a better product, especially as we're all working with these new developing AI models that are non-deterministic, you can't mock up all the states, and you can't theorize and you can't even make a clickable prototype with it. You sort of have to use the actual models underneath, and you have to see people try it out with their use cases, because with these models, you can design them for different use cases, but you actually discover use cases as you see people using them. So yes.
turns.zh: 我认为你得根据实际情况判断何时该上线产品，但我认为具备执行能力、用真实数据测试想法、以真实用户思维打造产品，这些确实能造就更出色的产品。尤其是在我们都在使用非确定性AI模型时，更需要这样做——你无法模拟所有可能的状态，无法进行理论推演，甚至无法用它制作可点击的原型。你只能依托实际模型观察用户如何应用，因为这些模型虽可针对不同场景设计，但用户实际使用时会发现更多应用场景。所以没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing I always hear, and building on what you just said is just you don't know what people will do with AI. You don't know how good it'll be at certain things, the non-deterministic piece of it. So you can create these amazing mocks of what it might be, and then people use it in a completely different way, which is where Cowork came from, and probably even Claude Code at the beginning. And so what's it just like to be a designer at Anthropic? Just give us a day in the life of working at Anthropic, at the center of the storm.
turns.zh: 我常听到的另一种说法（基于你刚才的观点）是，你无法预知人们会如何使用AI技术。你不知道它在某些任务上的表现会如何，尤其是在非确定性模型方面。你可以制作精美的模型原型，但用户可能以完全不同的方式使用它。这正是Cowork项目的起点，而Claude Code最初也面临过类似挑战。那么，在Anthropic做设计师是一种怎样的体验？请给我们讲讲你在Anthropic的日常工作——置身于风暴中心的日子。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: A good amount of time at Anthropic is actually just catching up on what's happening at the company. I think this is the company where ... I've worked at a few other companies around this size where I think there's just a lot of information and a lot of things going on, but I feel really compelled to keep up with it. There's stuff that is model developments on the research side. And then at any given time, there are just so many different teams prototyping and trying different ideas out, and there's a bunch of different code names and stuff like that. And a lot of time I'm just trying to navigate and figure out what those projects are, because I think I'm just trying to spot and see, hey, what's coming up ahead for me? Because there's stuff from both the research team, but also some of our labs teams that are closer to research, and trying out and prototyping stuff. (00:14:01): And then there's just stuff I want to try out. We have a bunch of prototypes and products internally that we can use, and I am just curious and I want to try those things out. And then I think there's also a lot of folks who internally have a lot of insights and opinions on where the industry's going. And some of those are just really interesting to read, because a lot of these are philosophical debates or directions of the company and stuff like that. And yeah, I feel like I just want to keep up with these things. Whereas I think in a normal company, I'm like, "It's fine. This is stuff that's happening outside of my reach. I don't really care as much." Where here, I think that it's both the volume and the kinds of things that are happening that I'm really interested in keeping up with. And then aside from that sort of keep up, that's not a huge part of my job, but I do think it's a really interesting part of it.
turns.zh: 在Anthropic公司，花大量时间其实就是了解公司的最新动态。我觉得这家公司……我曾在其他规模类似的公司工作过，那里信息量巨大、事务繁多，但我总觉得必须紧跟进展。研发部门有模型开发的进展；而在任何给定时间，总有多个不同团队在进行原型设计和探索新思路，还有各种代号项目之类的。很多时候我都在努力理清这些项目的脉络，因为我想预判未来可能面临的挑战。既有来自研发团队的信息，也有与研发更紧密合作的实验室团队在测试和验证新方案的动态。（00:14:01）此外，我还对内部的各种原型和产品充满好奇，迫切想亲自体验一番。公司内部许多人对行业发展趋势有着深刻见解，其中不乏富有哲理性的辩论或战略方向探讨，这些都让我深受启发，迫切想要持续关注。相比之下，在普通公司，我可能只会觉得“无所谓，这些都是超出我职权范围的事儿，我没那么在意”。但在这里，这种信息量和多样性实在太吸引人了，让我不由自主想要紧跟进展。尽管这并非我的核心职责，但我认为这部分工作也极具挑战性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, it connects to the point you made earlier, where a big part of the design role now is helping engineers and teams execute, not just telling them, "Here's the mock, here's the design." It's helping them stay on track, helping them connect ideas, create a cohesive experience as it's happening. So that makes sense.
turns.zh: 嗯，这和您之前提到的观点不谋而合——如今设计岗位的重要职责之一，就是帮助工程师和团队高效执行任务，而不只是简单地说：“这是设计稿，这是模型。”更重要的是要协助他们保持工作方向，串联各方思路，实时打造连贯的用户体验。这确实很有道理。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And I think part of it is just curiosity. It feels like I have this front row seat to so much that's happening in the industry. And so a lot of it is like, yeah, our Slack is a goldmine. I'm just excited to read through the things that people are working on, they're saying.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这背后还有好奇心的驱使。感觉自己仿佛坐在行业变革的前排，时刻关注着最前沿的动态。比如我们的Slack群组简直是个宝藏，每次翻阅大家正在进行的项目和讨论，都让我兴奋不已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I never thought about how there's already so much AI news to keep track of as a regular person. And then actually seeing what's actually happening inside a lab is a whole new set of feeds to watch.
turns.zh: 我从未意识到，作为普通人，要追踪的AI新闻量已经如此庞大。能亲眼见证实验室内部的真实研发进展，更是另一番令人着迷的视角。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I think that is the best AI news is probably internally, if you're ever at one of these companies in the Slack.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我觉得最棒的AI新闻可能还是在内部，如果你能在Slack上加入这些公司的讨论群的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Just problem keeps getting harder. I'm just keeping track of what's going on. Okay. Okay. So that's part of the job. What else?
turns.zh: 是啊。但问题是越来越难了。我只是在跟进进展。好的，好的。这也是工作的一部分。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: There is still some of the traditional, let me think about what's happening in the future and let me make some designs for that. That's something that, for example, this week I've allotted some time to, where I'm like, "Okay, cool. We have been in a lot of execution mode for Cowork, and now I want to set aside some time to think about, hey, what does the next three months look like, and where could that actually go given where the market's at, where the models are at, and what could that be?" Because I think it still really helps to visualize that and show that to the team, and point everyone in the same direction. And then I also spend a bunch of my day just jamming on stuff with engineers. A lot of it is just a conversation, or white boarding, or going through something that they built and giving them feedback on it and being a designer in that kind of way, we're really consulting. (00:16:39): And then I spend a part of my day in code, polishing, implementing stuff. Sometimes what happens is an engineer and I have worked through something and they've implemented a first version of it, and I just go in and polish it with them. And that's a really fun part of my job that I think didn't exist as much a few months ago.
turns.zh: 还是有一些传统的工作，我得想想未来会发生什么，再为此做些设计。比如这周我就抽出时间来做这件事，我会想：“好吧，不错。我们一直在为Cowork执行任务，现在我想留出一些时间来思考，接下来的三个月会是什么样子，考虑到市场现状和模型现状，可能会有哪些发展方向？”因为我觉得这对视觉化和向团队传达思路还是很有帮助的，能让大家朝着同一个方向努力。然后我一天中还有很多时间和工程师们一起探讨。这大多是交流、白板设计，或者查看他们开发的成果并提供反馈——以设计师的身份参与其中。我们其实是在提供咨询服务。（00:16:39）接下来我会花些时间写代码，进行优化和实现。有时候我和工程师一起完成初稿，然后再和他们一起优化。这部分工作真的很有趣，几个月前这种情况还不常见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you still doing elements of the traditional design process? Prototyping, user research, panels, I don't know, just going out and the whole thing you described?
turns.zh: 你还在做传统设计流程的部分吗？比如原型设计、用户研究、焦点小组讨论之类的？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, I think we're still doing all of that to some extent. We have a user researcher on the team who is putting together both traditional studies as well as surveys, and the whole team is reading those studies and that feedback. We are still prototyping stuff. I'm still mocking stuff up. I think it's just I have a wider set of tools now, and I think the proportion of time I spend doing each thing just has changed.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得我们在某种程度上还在做这些。我们团队里有用户研究员，她既做传统研究也做问卷调查，整个团队都会阅读这些研究报告和反馈。我们还在做原型设计。我还是会模拟一些东西。我觉得现在只是我的工具箱更丰富了，每个环节所占的时间比例有所变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. So that's a really interesting takeaway. It used to be that was a huge ... I guess what would be the pie chart of what your life was before, where it's like traditional thinking, planning, prototyping, mocking, research, and then just feedback and execution and out, today?
turns.zh: 明白了。好的。这真是个有趣的观察。以前你的生活可能是这样的，以传统思维为主，规划、原型设计、模拟、研究，然后反馈和执行，再到今天呢？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. I think as a designer a few years ago, I would say maybe 60 to 70% of it was mocking and prototyping stuff up, and then spending some of the last 20 or so doing the sort of jamming with engineers, consulting with them, and the last 10% maybe doing coordination meetings, et cetera. But now I feel like the mocking up part of it is 30 to 40%. And then there's that other 30 to 40% there that is now jamming and pairing directly with engineers. And then there's a slice, I don't know how much I have left, but there's a slice of it that is now implementation as well. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得几年前作为设计师，我可能60%到70%的时间都在模拟和原型设计，然后用剩下20%左右的时间和工程师们一起探讨、提供咨询，剩下10%可能用于协调会议之类的。但现在我感觉模拟部分占30%到40%。而现在和工程师直接合作、编码的部分占30%到40%。然后还有一部分，我不知道还剩多少，但现在也有实施的部分了。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually building and shipping?
turns.zh: 实际开发和上线吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So kind of following that thread, what's in your AI stack? What do you, as a designer, I know you're a manager and I want to talk about how you actually are IC also. What's in your AI stack? What tools are you using in your role?
turns.zh: 太棒了。接着上一个话题，你的AI技术栈里都有什么？作为设计师，我知道你现在是管理者，但我想聊聊你如何同时兼任IC角色。你的AI技术栈都有什么？你目前在职位上使用了哪些工具？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: What is in my AI stack? Well, we work at Anthropic, so we're going deep on the Claude stack. I'm using, obviously, chats, Claude Chat, but increasingly more and more Claude Cowork. I've basically shifted all of my chat use cases over to Cowork, because I've been finding that it sort of is better at these longer running tasks. And most of the things I was asking Claude for are these longer running tasks. (00:19:24): And then there's Claude Code, of course. I use it mostly with VS Code and the IDE because I'm usually tweaking front-end stuff, and it helps to just be able to see the code and then talk to Claude as well. I've been trying to actually use Claude Code more remotely, through both mobile and through Slack as well. It's really fun for somebody to say, "Oh yeah, this one icon's off or something," and you just at-mention Claude and Claude does it, and then you pick up the PR and it's done. That's been really, really fun too. (00:19:56): And yeah, I think we're a fully Claude house here. So yes, that's basically my stack.
turns.zh: 我的AI技术栈都有什么？嗯，我们在Anthropic工作，因此我们深度使用Claude技术栈。显然，我会用聊天功能，比如Claude Chat，但现在越来越多地使用Claude Cowork了。我基本上把所有聊天场景都转移到了Cowork上，因为我发现它在处理长期任务时更胜一筹。而我之前向Claude请求的大多是这类长期任务。（00:19:24）当然，还有Claude Code。我主要在VS Code和IDE中使用它，因为我经常调整前端内容，能够看到代码并与Claude对话非常方便。我一直在尝试远程使用Claude Code，通过手机和Slack实现。这真的很有趣，比如有人说：“哦，对，这个图标有问题之类的”，然后你@一下Claude，它就能处理好，最后你再接手PR就完成了。这真的非常有趣。（00:19:56）是的，我们这里完全是Claude为主。所以是的，这基本上就是我的技术栈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you still using Figma as a designer?
turns.zh: 你作为设计师还在使用Figma吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I am still using Figma, yes, yes.
turns.zh: 是的，我还在用Figma，是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I was waiting to hear. Okay. So Figma is still part of your life. Being a former Figmate, is that what y'all are called?
turns.zh: 好的，我等着听呢。好的。所以Figma仍然是你生活的一部分。作为前Figmate成员，你们是这么称呼自己的吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, Figmates, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，Figmates，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Okay. So I know there's this big debate on Twitter, just like, is code the future of design? Do we need many more, do we need a design? What's your sense? Figma's still important?
turns.zh: 是的。是的。好的。我知道推特上有个大讨论，比如代码是设计的未来吗？我们需要更多代码还是设计？你怎么看？Figma仍然重要吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I mean, as a former Figmate, maybe I'm biased in that way, but I think there is still ... When I use Figma, I'm like, "Yes, this is what I should be using." And it still fills a very good gap for me. I think a lot of that is actually just, one is exploring a lot of different options. I think that's a really important part of the design process, to be able to just think about 8 to 10 different ways to do something. I think the best design happens when you're able to just throw a bunch of ideas at the wall, and curate and push yourself to come up with a bunch of these different directions. Right now, coding, or right now working with some of these coding tools doesn't lend itself super well to that, because it's super linear, you get super invested in one direction and you just iterate with Claude on them, for example. (00:21:15): So Figma has been really great at just exploring all these different options, and I think it's still going to exist that way to some extent. And then I think there's really fine visual and interaction details that are also really great to be able to just try out in Figma. Again, it's a lot of different directions, but it's micro directions. It's being able to think about different typography or styles. Having those in a canvas where you can just explore that specifically is still so, so helpful, and is not something that I always want to go directly to code in.
turns.zh: 我是说，作为前Figmate成员，也许我对此有偏见，但我认为仍然有……当我使用Figma时，我会想：“对，这才是我应该用的工具。”它仍然为我填补了一个很好的空白。我认为很多时候实际上就是在探索不同的选项。这是设计过程中非常重要的一部分，能够思考8到10种不同的实现方式。我认为最好的设计发生在你能够把一堆想法抛向墙壁，然后筛选并推动自己想出各种不同方向的时候。现在编程，或者现在使用这些编程工具不太适合这样做，因为它太线性了，你会过于专注于一个方向，然后在Claude上进行迭代，例如。（00:21:15）所以Figma在探索所有这些不同选项方面非常棒，我认为它在某种程度上还会保持这种方式。然后我认为还有一些非常好的视觉和交互细节，也可以在Figma中尝试。再次强调，这有很多不同的方向，但都是微观方向。能够思考不同的排版或风格。在一个画布中专门探索这些仍然非常有帮助，而这不是我总是想直接转到代码中去做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting you still use an IDE, because in engineering, it's clearly shifting to command lines, agents, IDEs are kind of moving to not be cool anymore. And it makes a lot of sense. You just want to edit some CSS things, some color stuff. And so I could see why not just telling the agent, "Hey, just come on, change this one hex value." Just changing it is so much easier.
turns.zh: 真有趣，你居然还在用集成开发环境（IDE）。因为在工程领域，IDE显然正在让位于命令行和自动化工具，集成开发环境正逐渐过时。这其实很合理——你只想编辑一些 CSS 代码、调整颜色之类的东西。所以我能理解为什么不直接让自动化工具改动某个十六进制值，而是直接告诉它：“嘿，改成这个颜色就行。”这样操作简单得多。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. It's really annoying to be like, "Can you change this to this class?" When you can just go in and change it to a different class.
turns.zh: 是啊。当你想让别人把某个类改成另一个类时，却被要求“能不能把它改成这个类？”，这真的很烦人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's interesting. I wonder if IDEs now become the useful for designers and PMs, and engineers have moved on?
turns.zh: 所以这挺有意思的。我在想，现在 IDE 是否只适合设计师和产品经理，而工程师们已经抛弃了它们？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, maybe. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，或许吧。嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So a lot of your time you spend working with engineers, giving feedback, nudging them in the right direction. There's a sense, I feel, of just your advice is let go. Don't feel like you need to be this gatekeeper, but there's this piece of, okay, help them move in a direction that is cohesive and is creating products we're proud of. A lot of designers I think are in this boat right now, just like, "Oh my God, I can't keep up with all these engineers shipping stuff all day." What's something you learned about just either how to help your engineers get better at design so that it just ends up being better, or just keeping on top of this and not going crazy?
turns.zh: 好的。那你大部分时间都在和工程师合作，提供反馈，引导他们朝着正确的方向前进。我感觉你的角色更多的是提供建议，让他们顺势而为，而不是充当把关人。但关键在于，帮助他们朝着统一的方向前进，创造出令我们自豪的产品。现在很多设计师都深有同感，他们会感叹：“天哪，我根本跟不上这些工程师每天狂交代码的节奏。” 你有没有什么心得，能帮助工程师提高设计水平，或者至少能跟上进度，避免抓狂？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Whenever I do work with engineers on projects, and it's more on a consulting basis, I do just try to explain why I'm thinking a way that I'm thinking, to help them extract principles. As opposed to me just being like, "No, I don't think this should go here." It's like, "No, I think we should have a button here because not everybody realizes you can prompt this." And here's an example where it comes from research and whatnot. So I also just try to point engineers to our design system and stuff like that in code, because right now Claude is writing a lot of the code and it's not always picking up stuff in the design system and whatnot. So as much as I can equip them with stuff that they can use in the future without me, if that's helpful. (00:23:47): And then on your point of trying not to go crazy, I think it's hard. I think it's really hard right now. And I see this a lot from actually both engineers and designers, where it's like now that we're sort of capable of doing so much, we want to do more. And so I think it's not just designers who are feeling like, oh yeah, we have to keep up with engineers. I think even engineers are like, "How do we keep up with ourselves right now?" So that's something I'm hearing a lot.
turns.zh: 每次和工程师合作项目时，尤其是以咨询顾问的身份，我都会尽力解释我的设计思路，让他们提取其中的设计原则。而不是直接说“不，你不该把它放在这儿。” 比如，“不，我觉得这里应该加个按钮，因为不是所有人都意识到可以提示用户输入内容。” 我还会在代码中向他们展示我们的设计系统等资源，因为目前克劳德负责大量代码开发，但他并不总是能完全遵循设计系统的规范。所以只要能让他们掌握未来无需我协助就能运用的技能，那就是有益的。（00:23:47）：至于你提到的如何避免抓狂的问题，我觉得这很难。现在这对工程师和设计师来说都很难。我们现在能力太强了，总想做更多事。我觉得不只是设计师觉得要跟上工程师的节奏，甚至工程师自己也会说：“我们现在怎么跟上自己的节奏？” 这也是我常听到的声音。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So true. Oh man, how to keep up with all our agents, our seven agents we're constantly running?
turns.zh: 太对了。天哪，要怎么跟上我们那七个不断运转的代理程序？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So then as a designer where in this profession, craft and great experience and quality and trust are such a core part of the job, to help instill that in the products, because that in theory leads to really successful products in companies, how do you just think about maintaining craft quality, trust, as your products are just shipping 1,000 times a day, and you're not able to stay on top of them and there's no designer involved?
turns.zh: 好的。那作为设计师，在这个职业中，工艺、卓越的经验、质量和信任是核心要素。要如何在产品每天上线千次却无法亲自把控的情况下，保持工艺质量和信任感？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: It's not that there's no designer involved. It's more just like it's almost that there's too much for one designer to handle. But I think with this, I think about where the features or products are, where they are in the cycle of adoption versus early preview. So for example, we sometimes will launch things and we will say, "Hey, this is a research preview. It's early. It's going to have a bunch of these flaws," and we caveat that a bunch. I think Claude Cowork is actually a good example of this, where we labeled it a research preview and we put it out there knowing that, "Hey, this is similar to our models. This is the worst it's ever going to be, but we're going to put it out there because we believe, internally we've tried it a bunch, and there's something really powerful here that some people will benefit from. It might not yet be the easiest to work with. It might not be the highest quality. It might have some issues with it, but we're going to put it out there because we believe the benefits outweigh the cons." (00:25:49): I think that is okay to do, especially when there is something really valuable with the product already, and it's worth putting it out there. But I think the promise you sort of have to make your users is like, "Hey, we're going to put it out there, but we're going to iterate. We're going to take your feedback and we're going to iterate and we're going to make it better." And you have to commit that. You have to show that to the world, you have to respond to people's feedback, and you have to show that you are continuously shipping and improving it. Because I think the way that you really lose trust around quality and releasing something early, is if you release it early and then nothing ever happens. That is something that degrades a brand. (00:26:25): But whenever you put something out early, it's possible to do that and maintain the brand of your company. And I think that's something that we've been doing pretty well. And I think anyone who's listening can take away from it, it's like, yeah, well, we're continuing to do that. And I think that is actually really fun for me as a designer, because you put something out there and you actually learn and you get feedback about it immediately, and you know what to do next.
turns.zh: 并不是说没有设计师参与其中。更确切地说，是因为一个设计师要处理的工作量实在太大了。但我认为，在这种情况下，关键在于要清楚了解这些功能或产品所处的阶段——无论是处于采用周期还是早期预览阶段。比如，有时我们会推出产品并声明：“嘿，这只是一个研究预览版。它还很不成熟，会有很多缺陷。”我们会反复强调这些警示。Claude Cowork就是一个很好的例子。我们给它贴上“研究预览版”的标签，推出时就坦然告知用户：“嘿，这个产品和我们的现有模型类似。它目前可能还不够完善，但我们相信经过内部测试后，其中的一些核心功能会让部分用户受益。虽然它现在可能不太易用，质量也不尽如人意，存在一些问题，但我们依然决定将它推向市场，因为我们认为其带来的益处远大于缺点。”（00:25:49）我认为这种做法是可以接受的，尤其是在产品本身已经具备重大价值、值得推向市场的情况下。当然，我们必须向用户做出承诺：“我们会尽快迭代，收集用户反馈并持续改进。”你必须兑现这个承诺，向外界展示你的决心，积极回应用户反馈，并持续更新产品。毕竟，过早发布产品却后续毫无动静，才是真正损害品牌信誉的根源。（00:26:25）不过，通过早期发布并保持品牌声誉是完全可行的。我认为我们在这方面做得相当不错。听众朋友们也可以借鉴这一经验：是的，我们会继续坚持这种做法。对我这个设计师来说，这其实非常有趣——把产品推向市场后，你能即时获得反馈并进行迭代，知道下一步该怎么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I've heard you describe this is building trust through speed.
turns.zh: 据我所知，你对此的描述是通过速度来建立信任。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. Yeah, it's building trust through speed, but also just making people feel like they've been heard and that we're fixing things based on what they're trying to use it for, and their feedback is actually appreciated and used.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。通过速度建立信任，同时也要让用户感受到他们的声音被听到，我们会根据他们的使用场景和反馈进行改进，真正重视并采纳他们的意见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's clear when the labs launch stuff, and you all are very good at this, everyone on the team is tweeting and just responding to tweets and comments and then shipping, "Hey, we fixed this yesterday and this is happening." So there's a clear sense of, "This is just today and we know this is broke and we will fix it." And then because Claude Code can code very quickly, the fixes come very fast. (00:27:36): Okay. So another big question that people are asking that I ask a lot on this podcast, is around just what skills become valuable? And another way I've been thinking about it, Lex put it this way recently, is where will human brains continue to be valuable as AI gets smarter? So we've gone through this progression of tab completing [inaudible 00:27:56] segments of code, to 100% of code is written by AI now, it's crazy, to now AI is reviewing its own code. (00:28:04): Boris on the podcast recently was saying Claude Code is now helping them come up with ideas and decide what to build, which is like, okay, wow, look at that. Look at it go. The whole product workflows, the product development process slowly get eaten up by AI. So the question is just where will human brains still be useful, at least until we have super intelligence? Do you think AI is going to get very, very good at taste, judgment, design?
turns.zh: 是啊，每当实验室推出新产品时，大家都能看得一清二楚。团队里的每个人都会在推特上积极互动、回复评论，然后发布消息：“嘿，我们昨天修复了这个问题，现在又出现新情况了。” 这种清晰的沟通节奏让人一目了然：“这事儿今天刚出，我们知道它有问题，会尽快修复。” 而Claude Code的开发速度极快，修复进度自然也很迅速。（00:27:36）：好的。还有个大家常问、我自己在播客里也常探讨的大问题——哪些技能会变得越来越有价值？Lex最近提到的一个观点让我深有共鸣：随着AI越来越智能，人类大脑的价值何在？我们见证了代码补全的演进，从手动编写代码，到现在100%由AI完成编码，简直不可思议，再到现在AI开始自审代码。（00:28:04）：Boris最近在播客中提到，Claude Code现在还能帮助他们构思产品方案、决定开发方向。这真是令人惊叹的进展。整个产品工作流程、产品开发过程正逐渐被AI侵蚀。那么问题来了：至少在超级智能到来之前，人类大脑还有哪些价值？你觉得AI在审美、判断和设计方面会变得非常出色吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I think it will get better at taste and judgment and design. Yeah, I think we might be holding onto that a little bit too much and saying, "Oh yeah, a designer or somebody will always know the best thing to ship or the best version of this." But I do think AI's sense of taste will get better. At the end of the day, someone has to decide what is actually going to get built and what actually matters. And when I think about people saying, "Oh, AI is just going to build this software for us," a lot of the hard parts of building software are actually not building it. If you think about the hardest times that you've had at work, Lenny, it's probably things like, oh, you and some other person disagreeing about what should go into this feature or what shouldn't go into this feature. (00:29:20): And those things still feel like, yes, AI can weigh in, but it can't necessarily solve this dispute between you and somebody else. And so there is something about deciding what actually goes into the things we build, which I guess is taste in some way, but maybe not taste in the way we think about aesthetic taste or whatnot. There's some sort of, it's judgment around what to do next.
turns.zh: 我认为它们在审美、判断和设计方面会越来越强。是啊，我们可能还在过于依赖人类的经验，心想：“设计师总能找到最佳上线方案、最完美的产品版本。” 但我相信AI的审美能力会不断提升。归根结底，总得有人决定最终上线的内容和重点优先级。当人们说“AI会替我们开发软件”时，我觉得这话说得太轻易了。软件开发中最困难的部分往往不是编码本身。如果你回想自己工作中最头疼的时刻，Lenny，比如你和同事争论某个功能该加入还是排除，这些问题依然存在。（00:29:20）：AI可以提供参考意见，但无法解决你们之间的分歧。决定产品最终形态的过程，某种程度上就是审美判断，但可能不是我们通常理解的审美标准。这里需要的是对下一步行动的明智判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just watching how quickly AI took over coding, which, I think a year ago, definitely two years ago, most people are like, "I don't think so. I don't think AI will get this good." And that the best engineers in the world trusted so much, they're not even looking at the code anymore. That's where we've gone. It just made me reevaluate all these assumptions I've had about, okay, AI will never be as good as really good PMs, designers, at judging what is great and deciding what to build. But I'm just starting to think, I think it will get there. Even an example you've shared, it could give these two people trying to make a decision, "Here's all of the data you need to make a decision and here's why this is the right answer and just press yes, press one, and I'll go ahead and build this." (00:30:31): So I think to your point, I think we undervalue just how good it'll get at this stuff. Okay. So your sense is it'll get better, but your sense is we'll still need awesome designers to be involved, us and PMs, to help make these decisions, engineers, of course?
turns.zh: 看看AI多快就接管了编程工作。我记得一年前、两年前，多数人还说“我不这么认为。AI不可能做到这么出色”。而如今，全球顶尖工程师都深信不疑，甚至不再亲自审阅代码了。这就是我们如今的现状。这让我重新审视了自己的一些固有假设——比如，AI永远无法比得上真正优秀的产品经理和设计师在判断产品价值、决策构建方向方面的能力。但我现在开始觉得，它终究会达到那个水准。就拿你提到的例子来说，AI可以为两位决策者提供所有必要数据，解释为何某个方案是正确答案，然后直接按下“是”或“1”即可。（00:30:31）所以我认为，正如你所说，我们低估了AI在这些领域的潜力。好的，那么你的观点是，AI会不断进步，但我们仍需要优秀的设计师、产品经理和工程师共同参与决策，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I think someone will still have to decide, oh, we want to build this kind of product. Or given what the AI is presenting us, someone still needs to be accountable for the decision. The same way that even though Claude can write all this code for you today, it is still an engineer who's accountable for, does that code actually work? Does this actually make sense in the product? So I think there's that decision making/judgment layer, which feels like maybe one day will come when we won't have to do that, but it still falls on us. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我觉得总得有人来做决定，比如“我们要开发这种产品”。或者在AI给出方案后，仍需有人为最终决策负责。就像现在Claude能帮你写代码，但最终还是工程师要验证代码是否有效、是否符合产品逻辑。所以我认为决策/判断层面依然存在。或许未来某天我们无需亲自做这些决策，但现在这仍是我们的责任。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It doesn't make sense. It makes me think about the radiology example, where there's always the sense that AI is going to take over that field of radiology and tell you what is going on. But the human is mostly useful for signing off on the decision, because someone needs to be liable if they're wrong. Which isn't the best job in the world, but that's a different game as [inaudible 00:31:38] code.
turns.zh: 这说不通。这让我想到放射科的例子，人们总觉得AI会接管这个领域，告诉你病变情况。但实际上人类主要负责签字确认，因为如果诊断错误，责任必须由人承担。这份工作不算理想，但和编写代码完全是两码事。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another ongoing question in AI and design is just, it feels like chatbots and terminals are just like, I don't think anyone expected this to be the lasting user interface to AI. Chatbots, okay, no, no, this is just a temporary stop along the journey, but now it's gone even further, and just terminals. Do you have thoughts on just, I don't know, do you think there will be a next step of how we interface with AI, or do you think chatbots and terminals are mostly where we end up?
turns.zh: 好的。AI和设计领域的一个持续讨论点是，聊天机器人和终端界面似乎成了主流。人们原本以为这只是AI的临时交互方式，但现在它们已深入人心。你对此有何看法？你认为AI的交互方式会有下一步突破，还是觉得聊天机器人和终端界面就是终极形态？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: There will likely be a combination of both, both UIs and interfaces that you are interacting with, clicking with, and that feel more tactile., We are already seeing this and playing with this within Claude, the chatbot. So we recently released a bunch of these widgets that let Claude elicit and ask you questions, and also show you things like the weather and stocks and whatnot in interactive ways. And I think those have had a really good reception, because people still like to see UIs and touch them and click them, and they are much more efficient than typing something to Claude. But at the same time, when we really leaned into this chatbot paradigm, I think that just gave us this whole world of flexibility that we didn't get with these sort of baked-in UIs. So my read here is I don't think Chat is ever going away because this opened up this new way of infinite ways to work with the model, and to talk to the computer, that we just didn't have before. (00:33:17): But I think that it will still be most direct for very specific things to exist in this UI. And I think that what will probably happen here, is that a lot of those UIs will be generated more and more often by the models, as opposed to something that we're hand coding each instance. But I think we're in this space where I don't think chat ... And maybe even talking to the terminal is going to go away.
turns.zh: 很可能两者会结合起来，即你正在与之交互、点击的用户界面（UI）和界面，会让人感觉更具触觉性。我们已经在Claude聊天机器人中看到了这一点，并对此进行了探索。因此，我们最近发布了一系列小部件，让Claude能够提问并向你展示天气、股票等信息，以交互式方式呈现。我认为这些功能反响良好，因为人们仍然喜欢看到UI界面、触摸它们并进行点击操作，这比向Claude输入文字高效得多。但与此同时，当我们真正深耕聊天机器人模式时，我认为这为我们带来了前所未有的灵活性空间，而这种灵活性是传统固有UI所无法比拟的。所以我的看法是，聊天功能不会消失，因为它开辟了与模型互动、与计算机对话的无限可能性——这些可能性在此之前都是不存在的。（00:33:17）但我认为对于非常特定的任务，使用这种UI界面仍会是最直接的选择。我认为未来很可能出现的情况是，许多UI界面将由模型自动生成，而非手动编写每个实例。但我认为我们正处于这样一个阶段——我不认为聊天……甚至与终端对话会消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that with OpenClaw, Claude, Moltbot, all the names, one of the big innovations is another way to chat with it through WhatsApp and Telegram and SMS, just like another form of chatbot, but just like, that was a big [inaudible 00:33:54]. Oh, I could just chat with it through WhatsApp.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，通过OpenClaw、Claude、Moltbot等名字，我们看到一个重大创新点是通过WhatsApp、Telegram和短信等平台与它们聊天的新方式，就好像是另一种聊天机器人形式，但这确实是一个重大突破[00:33:54]。哦，我甚至可以通过WhatsApp与它聊天。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. And it's like chatting and talking to someone is still ... We as humans are doing it, and it's a way for us to interact in a really rich way. And now we just have this other medium to interact with a computer, basically.
turns.zh: 是的。聊天和与人交谈仍然……我们人类就是这样做的，这是一种非常丰富的人际互动方式。现在我们只是有了一种与计算机交互的另一种媒介，基本上就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So Kevin Wheel, who works at another AI lab I won't mention, he had this great point on the podcast that talking is such a beautiful way to handle every level of intelligence. We can talk to people that are very, very smart and not so smart and it's talking, and it scales so well across the spectrum. We can talk to people at 200 IQ, 300, like its talking still works. So that's why it's been this beautiful way to deal with the growing intelligence of models as it continues to work.
turns.zh: 是的。所以在另一个我不便透露名字的AI实验室工作的Kevin Wheel在播客中提出了一个很棒的观点：交谈是处理各种智能水平的绝佳方式。我们可以与非常聪明的人和不太聪明的人交谈，而且交谈方式非常灵活，适用于不同层次的智能。我们可以与智商200、300的人交谈，交谈方式依然有效。因此，这就是为什么它成为处理不断增长的模型智能的绝佳方式，因为它能随着模型智能的提升而持续发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, that totally makes sense. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，这完全说得通。是的。
