turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, I have takes on this. Yeah. So this past year at Anthropic, I joined as an IC at first, and then I managed a team for a few months in an org structure that sort of needed it, and now I'm actually back to doing full-time IC work. And I joined Anthropic as an IC because I was just really excited about the kind of work that there was to be done as an IC here, but also because I was feeling like I sort of want to be closer to the work, and I think this feels like a really important time to do it, before I ascend the corporate ranks. And I was having these questions and doubts about, is middle management, is that safe in the future? Is the way that we're working actually, is this going to be a job that persists in the future? Or should I try something else and get my hands dirty kind of thing? (00:36:47): And to be totally fair, I actually love both sides of the coin. I love managing people. I love setting up teams and being at that level, but I also just really love IC work. I was sort of a reluctant manager when I did it, and I was like, "Okay, I'll do it." So I love both sides of the coin pretty equally. But I think actually what being an IC across this past year has taught me, is that it actually just gave me a lot of skills that I don't think I would've gained if I was just managing throughout this year. Like I mentioned, the design process has changed so, so much in this past year, and I feel like I've just picked up so many hard skills that I wouldn't have necessarily had the time to do if I was just managing a team. So that's actually the best thing it's afforded me. (00:37:31): And I think at any point if I'm managing a team again, I think it will give me the empathy and understanding of how the design process has changed. And I think that's actually a really important thing right now because the teams are working so differently. And I think it's actually pretty hard to empathize if you are not working in that way, or you're not always testing all the tools and trying stuff. But yeah, it's an interesting time to be a designer. And if I had not worked in this environment, I don't know if I would've totally understood it or knew what to do or how to guide my teams. So that's sort of what this year really gave me.
turns.zh:
是的，我对此有一些看法。过去一年在Anthropic，我先是以IC身份加入，后来在一个需要IC角色的组织结构中管理团队几个月，现在又回归全职IC工作。我选择加入Anthropic是因为我对这里IC岗位的工作内容充满热情，同时也想更贴近实际业务，尤其是在晋升职级前抓住这个重要机遇。当时我对中层管理的未来存疑：这种工作模式能否持续？或者我是否该尝试其他更接地气的方向？（00:36:47）说实话，我两边都喜欢。我喜欢管理团队，搭建团队架构，但也热爱IC工作。当我担任管理者时，内心其实有些抗拒，总觉得“好吧，我先做着吧”。所以我对两者同样重视。但过去一年担任IC的经历让我收获了许多管理工作无法给予的技能。比如，过去一年设计流程发生了巨大变革，我借此掌握了许多实用技能，否则在管理团队时根本无暇顾及。这正是最大的收获。
（00:37:31）我相信如果未来再度管理团队，这些经验将帮助我更好理解设计流程的变化。鉴于当前团队工作模式差异巨大，这一点至关重要。若不亲身实践，缺乏同理心和试错机会，管理团队时必然力不从心。所以现在设计师面临着挑战。如果没有这段经历，我恐怕难以完全理解现状，也无从指导团队。总之，过去一年给了我太多启发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so you were previously a director of design at Figma, right?
turns.zh: 你之前是Figma的设计总监，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How big was your team? How large was your org, just to give people a reference?
turns.zh: 你们团队规模有多大？你们公司的规模有多大，方便给我们参考一下吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: At the max, I probably had, I think, 12, 15 designers or so, and I had a few managers as well.
turns.zh: 最多的时候，我大概有12到15名设计师，还有几位经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then you went back to an IC?
turns.zh: 不错。那之后你又回到了独立贡献者（IC）的角色？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: It was like an org.
turns.zh: 那是个组织。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So you had the sense that middle management might not last. What's your current feeling? Do you think design management is a thing that persists long-term, or do you think everyone turns into IC?
turns.zh: 是的。好的。所以你觉得中层管理可能无法长久存在。现在你有什么看法？你认为设计管理是可以长期持续的职位，还是大家最终都会转成IC？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I think as long as there is a team of people, it helps to have somebody who is managing a team. I think there's real value in managers. It depends what the shape of the manager is and what they actually do. But the way I think about what a helpful manager is these days, is somebody who is not just, I think pure people management like, oh, just somebody to set you up, help you in your career, have one-on-ones, make sure you're feeling good at work. I think that that is not a thing as much anymore, but I think somebody who can really function as giving the team direction, as well as doing some of the people management stuff, that tied together, I think is the future of what managing looks like, at least for now. Somebody who can really engage with the team in terms of the work and giving direction there, as well as creating the environment for them to do their best work.
turns.zh: 我觉得只要有团队，就需要有人来管理团队。经理确实有其价值。这取决于经理的角色定位和实际职责。但就我目前对有效经理的理解，他们不应只是纯粹的人力管理——比如，仅仅安排工作、帮助职业发展、一对一沟通、确保工作环境良好之类的。这种传统模式已经过时了。如今有价值的经理应该是既能为团队指明方向，又能处理人力管理事务的复合型角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And do you see yourself going back into management long-term?
turns.zh: 那你认为自己未来会长期重返管理岗位吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I will. I probably will. I think I really just love helping a team build the best product possible. And my motto there is, whatever it takes. If it's somebody that, if the team needs somebody to give the team direction and set up the team and whatnot, that could be me. If the team just needs somebody to execute on it, that could be me as well.
turns.zh: 会的。我可能会的。我真的很喜欢帮助团队打造出最棒的产品。我的座右铭是，不惜一切代价。如果团队需要有人来指导、组建团队之类的，那可以是我。如果团队只需要执行者，那也可以是我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice I'm hearing for people in design that are especially managers, is you almost need to move back into IC in order to truly understand what is happening and how much it's changing, so that you can be a better manager.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的建议是，特别是设计领域的经理们，应该先回归IC角色，真正理解行业变化和趋势，这样才能成为更出色的管理者。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I think so. And I think traditionally, at least what I've seen, a lot of the engineering disciplines, when they hire EMs or even sometimes directors there, they actually make the EMs take a rotation for a few months and pick up a few tasks, and really understand how the technology works before they become a full-time manager. And I think design probably needs to do something similar too, where I think in the past design has been much more people management oriented.
turns.zh: 我觉得是的。传统上，至少我观察到，许多工程部门在招聘EM甚至有时是总监时，都会让他们先轮岗几个月，参与技术开发，真正理解技术原理后再转为全职管理者。我认为设计领域也需要类似的做法。过去设计更多聚焦于人力管理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you find yourself most rusty in when you went back to IC designer?
turns.zh: 你回归IC设计师后，发现自己最生疏的是什么？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Actually doing crits, and just really-
turns.zh: 实际上，做点评环节，还有就是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Getting criticized.
turns.zh: 被点评。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: ... Yeah, getting criticized. You're like, oh yeah, it is hard to get critical feedback and to hear it, and to hear it on such a regular basis, because that's the thing you have to do as a designer, is it's a pretty vulnerable exercise to share work and present it with your team, and then also just get a lot of critical feedback and take that all the time. Yeah.
turns.zh: ……是的，被点评。你会意识到，获得批评性反馈并接受它真的很难，尤其是当这种反馈频繁出现时。因为作为设计师，这就是你必须做的事——与团队分享和展示作品，然后接受大量批评并不断改进。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So currently you're leading design/IC designing on cowork. Is that right?
turns.zh: 嗯，目前你在Cowork项目中负责设计/集成电路设计，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So Boris, he was on the pod recently, talked about how there's a lot of debate about what cowork should be, and there's all these big ideas and he's like, "In the end, let's just make it like a terminal, basically, in the product, and just kind of a fancy terminal." Is there anything you could share about just the process of landing on where you landed for that experience of cowork? I have it here on my monitor, by the way, looking at it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Boris最近在播客里谈到，关于Cowork应该是什么样子有很多争议，有各种各样的宏大构想。他最后说：“最终，我们就把它做成一个终端，基本上就是产品里的一个终端，弄个花哨的终端。”关于Cowork的设计过程，你能分享一下吗？顺便说一下，我现在正在显示器上看相关内容。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: With Cowork specifically, we have had a bunch of different prototypes internally of what that could look like. And it's one of those things where we tried a lot of things, and then I think we weren't really sure when it was actually going to be ready to ship. And then it was sort of everything all at once. We were like, "Okay, we're going to ship it soon."
turns.zh: 关于Cowork，我们内部做了很多不同的原型设计。当时我们尝试了很多方案，但不确定什么时候能真正上线，最后就把所有东西整合起来了。当时我们就想：“好吧，我们很快就要上线了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it was 10 days, 10 days of building.
turns.zh: 我记得用了10天时间。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, it was definitely longer than that overall. It was 10 days to get it from what we had internally to something that we were ready to ship externally. So we'd been building it for a while, but we weren't really sure about the actual form it was going to take. And so the way it got there is actually, there was a lot of different other explorations that we had internally on top of different agent harnesses and whatnot. And we just had prototyped little parts of the different interactions that ended up in cowork. So things like when Claude gives you a to do list, we tried a bunch of different form factors for that. We tried a bunch of different form factors for the way it presents you different multiple choice questions. We tried a bunch of different ways to teach people what the use cases are and whatnot. (00:42:38): And I don't know if we landed on the best form factor ever, but essentially it was stuff that was already working internally that people liked, that we just thought we were going to get some more signal on by releasing it. So I think forcing ourselves to release it within that 10 days that we did, it was just sort of like, whatever we had, let's put it out there and then let's go out there and iterate from there, which is what we're doing.
turns.zh: 是的，总体来说时间更长。从内部设计到能对外发布的版本，花了10天时间。所以我们开发了很久，但不确定最终的形态。实现的过程中，我们在内部尝试了各种不同的交互方式，比如Claude给你的待办列表、多项选择题的呈现方式，还有用户指导等功能。（00:42:38）我不确定我们是否找到了最佳方案，但基本上都是内部已经验证过的设计，只是想通过发布获得更多反馈。所以我们在10天内强制上线，就是把现有内容推出去，然后再根据用户反馈迭代，这就是我们现在在做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it blew up the internet when you launched it, so it worked out.
turns.zh: 你们上线后在网上反响很好，结果很成功。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a feature of Cowork today that you're either most proud of, or just can't wait to fix and improve?
turns.zh: Cowork现在有没有哪个功能是你最引以为傲的，或者最迫不及待想改进的？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Honestly, I think I'm just most proud of us actually just shipping it, to be honest, and putting it out there. And yeah, I don't know if there's one specific thing yet, because I think when you work on something and you work at so long, especially as a designer, you're like, I don't know. All I can do is see flaws in it, but I think there's a lot of stuff that I'm excited about. We have been iterating, especially on the homepage, and to make that something where it feels more like, "Hey, these are tasks you can give Claude and the tasks that Claude are working on. " And so that actually should be rolling out. It might already be rolled out by the time this comes out.
turns.zh: 说实话，我最自豪的还是我们最终把它上线了。还有，我也不确定有没有特别突出的功能，因为作为设计师，工作太久后，总会看到各种缺点，但确实有很多让我兴奋的地方。我们一直在迭代，尤其是主页部分，让它更符合用户需求，比如“这些是可以交给Claude的任务，以及Claude正在处理的任务”。这个改进应该很快就会上线了，可能等这期播客发布时就已经完成了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see this little randomizer thing, where you click it and gives you all these different ideas.
turns.zh: 我看到这个随机生成器的东西，你点击它，它就会给你各种各样的想法。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And then so when you actually start to work with Claude on stuff, it feels more like a to do list. It feels more like these are things Claude's working on, these are things that Claude needs your attention on. And I think there's an opportunity here to make it feel much more like this shared to do list between you and Claude. So excited to iterate on that. And then I'm also excited to think more about what is the actual true form factor of this? Is it stuck in this screen always, or how does this reach out to the different surfaces that it's working with?
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。当你真正开始和Claude一起做事时，感觉更像是一个待办清单。感觉更像是Claude正在处理的事情，这些都是Claude需要你关注的。我认为这里有机会让它更像是你和Claude之间的共享待办清单。很期待对此进行改进。然后我也很兴奋能进一步思考这个东西的实际形态是什么。它是永远停留在这个屏幕上，还是能扩展到它所工作的不同界面？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you shared that it wasn't just 10 days to do this thing. There's these numbers that people throw out there, "We built it in 10 days." And your point is there was time spent thinking about what direction it should go, and prototyping, mocking, trying stuff. And then it's like, okay, now we know what we want it to be. Let's build it and ship it.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你提到这件事不只是用了10天时间完成的。人们常抛出一些数字，比如“我们在10天内就把它做出来了”。你的观点是，花了时间思考它应该朝哪个方向发展，还进行了原型设计、模拟、尝试各种方案。然后就是，好，现在我们知道我们想要它成为什么样子。那就建造它并发布吧。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. I think for some reason that became the viral thing that got taken away from all of the cowork announcements, is that it only took 10 days, but I think there have just been so many different explorations, and people that have worked on different pieces of cowork, that it was not just 10 days, and there was a lot of different people involved. It's one of those things where it's like the idea kept coming back, and it's never the right moment or there's different variations of it, and then all of a sudden it's the right moment and it feels like, oh, so obvious all along, but there was a long, long journey to get there.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得不知为何，这成了病毒式传播的内容，盖过了所有关于Cowork的公告，人们只记得用了10天时间，但实际上有太多的探索过程，有太多人参与了Cowork的不同部分。这不只是10天的时间，还有很多不同的人参与其中。这就像是一个不断浮现的想法，但总没有合适的时机，或者有不同的变体，然后突然间时机成熟了，一切都豁然开朗，但其实这是一个漫长的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And by the way, for people that don't know much about cowork, the way I think about it, it's like Claude with hands, or to do stuff on your computer. How would you describe it, just in a sentence or two?
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，对于不了解Cowork的人来说，我对它的理解是，Claude就像有手的助手，或者说是在你的电脑上做事的助手。你能用一两句话描述一下吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: That's a good description. I actually haven't heard that, but I like that. I might use it more often as Claude with hands. I also think about it as it's like Claude, but Claude is really good at taking all your garbage and then turning it into something nice. I think one of my favorite, any sort of use case that I really like out of cowork, is just giving it a folder of my stuff, and it doesn't really matter what's in that folder, but I'm able to extract something good out of it.
turns.zh: 这个描述很棒。我其实还没听过这种说法，但我喜欢。我可能会更常用“Claude有手了”这个说法。我还觉得它就像Claude，但Claude特别擅长把你所有的烂摊子变成好东西。我认为我在Cowork中最喜欢的用例之一，就是给它一个文件夹，里面放些东西，不管里面有什么，但我总能从中提取出一些好的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've done that many times. Okay. Coming back to managing and being a manager and the role of a designer, I'm going to talk about hiring for a little bit. So seeing how much is changing in the role of a designer, what do you look for that's maybe new? What do you now look for when you're hiring designers, that you think is really important for them to be successful in this new world?
turns.zh: 我已经这么做过很多次了。好的。回到管理和当经理以及设计师的角色，我要谈谈招聘方面。看到设计师的角色在发生如此大的变化，你认为有什么新的要求呢？在招聘设计师时，你现在会寻找哪些你认为对他们在新世界中取得成功至关重要的特质？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Well, I do think working specifically in the kind of environment that I do, there's just a sense of resilience and roll with it, kind of thing, that I think is really important because so much is changing around us and you have to be really willing to adapt, to try out new methods, to try out new tools and learn stuff, as opposed to just be stuck in the old processes and the old ways. But then I think about also, there's probably three archetypes of folks that are really interesting to me right now. And I think these folks were already interesting to me before, but I feel like in this era feels especially important. (00:47:05): So the first one I would call is strong generalists. So not just regular generalists where they're kind of good at a lot of things, but people that are almost block shaped, in that T-shaped framework, where it's like they're really good at a few core skills, like 80th percentile good. I think this is pretty rare and hard to hire for, to be honest, but I like this because the design role we've already seen is stretching and spanning. We're all becoming more PM shape, we're all becoming engineering shaped. And so if you already have strong skills in a few different buckets, it's really easy for you to flex around and expand your role. So that's really exciting to me. It's just somebody who is really good at a bunch of things, again, a huge ask. (00:47:56): And then the other person that's really exciting to me, is in that T-shaped framework, a deep specialist, someone who is T-shaped, but the tip of the T probably goes down farther than most other people. So folks that are maybe the top 10% in the industry and whatnot. Again, super hard to find. And I feel very lucky that working at some of these places, folks like these, you could sort of afford to hire them and actually bring them on board. (00:48:27): And then my last one is probably the one that I think we're all overlooking, which is what I call the craft new grad. It's just somebody who's early career and feels, like, wise and experienced beyond their years, but is also just very humble and very eager to learn. And I think this person is really interesting right now because I think most companies are just hiring senior talent, folks that have done things before, are super experienced, but given how much the roles are changing and what we're expected to do is changing, I think having somebody who almost has a blank slate, and is just a really quick learner and is really eager to learn new tactics and stuff like that, and doesn't have all these baked in processes and rituals in their mind, that's super valuable. So I think those are the folks that I think a lot of us are just overlooking, but I'm really excited about.
turns.zh: 嗯，我确实认为，在我所处的这种工作环境中，人们需要具备一种韧性和随机应变的能力。我认为这非常重要，因为我们周围的一切都在不断变化，你必须愿意去适应新事物，尝试新方法，学习新技能，而不是固守旧有的流程和习惯。但我同时也注意到，目前有三种类型的人让我特别感兴趣。其实这些人以前就让我感兴趣，但在当下这个时代，他们显得尤为重要。（00:47:05）：首先，我要提到的类型是强大的通才。他们不只是普通的多面手，而是那种T型人才框架中的典范。他们在某些核心技能上达到80%的卓越水平。这类人才确实很难找到，招聘难度极大，但我很欣赏他们。因为我们已经看到，设计岗位的职责正在不断延伸和拓展。我们都在向项目经理的方向转型，工程师的技能要求也在提升。因此，如果你已经在多个领域掌握了深厚的技能，就能轻松地拓展自己的角色。这让我很兴奋。不过，要成为这样的全才，要求实在太高了。（00:47:56）：接下来让我兴奋的是另一种T型人才——深度专家。他们在某个领域达到行业前10%的水平，但他们的T型框架中的尖端技能可能比大多数人更深厚。这种人才极其难得。我很幸运能在某些公司工作，遇到这样的优秀人才，公司愿意为他们提供平台。（00:48:27）：最后一种类型或许是我们都忽视了的——我称之为"新晋手艺人"。他们初入职场，却表现得比同龄人更智慧、更有经验，同时又非常谦逊，求知若渴。我认为这种人才在当下特别重要，因为大多数公司都在招聘资深人才，即那些经验丰富、能力成熟的人。但随着职位职责不断变化，要求不断提高，拥有一张白纸般的思维，学习新技能的能力，以及快速适应新策略的意愿，变得尤为珍贵。因此，我认为这些人才是我们都容易忽视的，但我对他们充满期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. On the deep T shape, what's an example of someone in design that has a ... What's a skill that they're really good at?
turns.zh: 太棒了。关于深度T型人才，能举个设计领域的例子吗？他们在哪个技能上特别出色？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Sometimes there's designers who are just really technical in a way where they could be 50% of ... they're basically a software engineer. That's really interesting, especially because right now a lot of it is, at least for us, it's like you're working directly with the model, so it helps when you have just deep engineering expertise. But another deep specialist T is just maybe they're just really good at visual design or just designing icons or something, where things like that, given that anybody can make anything, having that deep specialist slant feels like, oh yeah, they can really help differentiate the things that we're building.
turns.zh: 有时候，有些设计师在技术层面非常出色，他们甚至可以称得上是50%的……他们基本上就是软件工程师。这真的很有趣，尤其是现在很多情况下，至少对我们而言，就是直接与模型打交道，所以拥有深厚的工程技术专长确实很有帮助。但另一些深层专业人才可能只是在视觉设计或图标设计方面非常擅长——毕竟任何人都能做出一些东西，但若具备这种深层的专业专长，就会让人觉得，哦，他们确实能让我们的产品与众不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. And then there's block shape. We had Mark Andrews on the podcast, we kind of called it the F shape or E shape, where there's multiple T things, sideways F, sideways E, I guess. Is that what you're describing, where there's many things you're really, really good at?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。然后还有块状人才。我们在播客上邀请了Mark Andrews，我们把这种人才称作F形或E形，就是有很多T形人才，侧着的F形，侧着的E形之类的。你描述的这种情况，是指他们在很多领域都非常非常擅长吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And basically, I don't know, if you almost had their skillset, it would look like a block instead of a T.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。基本上，我不知道，如果你几乎拥有他们的技能组合，看起来就会像一个块状人才而不是T形人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because there's so many skills that the T is spread out.
turns.zh: 因为T形人才的技能太分散了。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And the crack new grad. So this is just someone that is eager, open-minded, gritty, very smart, I imagine is a big part of it.
turns.zh: 好的。还有新晋毕业生。我想这些新人必须要积极进取、思想开放、意志坚定、非常聪明，这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone's a young designer trying to break in, trying to be successful, what would your advice be to them to help them have a shot at joining Anthropic, for example?
turns.zh: 如果有年轻设计师想进入这个行业，想要成功，你会给他们什么建议，让他们有机会加入Anthropic这样的公司呢？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I would just say just build a bunch of stuff, try a bunch of stuff out, build actual things. I think that can feel ... I don't really know what the state of design education or education is these days, but at least from back when I was in school, everything was very theoretical, and here, we're going to teach you some approaches and whatnot. But the best crack new grad folks I know are just people who just use the technology, build actual things, don't feel limited by how little experience they might have. I think that sometimes they're actually unburdened by that, because we have expectations of ourselves after being in the industry for so long, but they actually don't and they sort of feel like anything is possible. And so just building a bunch of stuff and sharing it with people, and finding a community of folks that also do that. (00:51:50): Yeah. I think my one call it here too, is I went to a school that started something called Socratica a few years after, actually a while after I graduated. And basically their whole thing is building stuff and showcasing it almost like a science project. And I think there's just been a really cool movement there of folks who just build things and do things. For example, somebody built this Claude robot project, this was a few years ago too, where they were just assembling robots that were running on Claude, and then somebody else did something where she just wanted to put Googly eyes on a bus in Boston or something. And there's just a sense of both agency in terms of, yeah, we can just do stuff, but then also this community where people were just trying and building things and sharing things with each other. So whatever that looks like, given the school that someone's from or graduating from, doing that kind of stuff is the stuff that will make people stand out.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，多尝试、多动手实践，真正去创造一些东西。我觉得这感觉……我不太清楚当下设计教育的现状，但至少在我上学那会儿，一切都太理论化了。现在我们会教你一些方法之类的，但我认识的最优秀的新晋设计师，就是那些直接运用技术、实际动手制作的人，他们并不受自身经验不足的限制。我觉得有时候他们反而更轻松，因为我们在行业里待久了会给自己设限，但他们没有这些束缚，觉得一切皆有可能。所以多动手实践，向他人展示成果，找到志同道合的伙伴。（00:51:50）：是啊。我也想说，我毕业后不久，学校推出了一个叫Socratica的项目。他们的理念就是动手创造，像做科学项目一样展示成果。我觉得那里有股很棒的风气——人们不断尝试、动手制作。比如，有人做了Claude机器人项目，那是几年前的事了，他们组装机器人，让Claude驱动运行。还有人想在波士顿公交车上贴上大眼睛。那种自主感很强——既能动手创造，又能在社区里分享成果。无论出身哪所学校，毕业生只要能做到这些，就能脱颖而出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For current designers that are [inaudible 00:52:54] career, [inaudible 00:52:55] senior, do you think that you need to get technical and learn to code, at least build, or do you think you could be really successful and just not lean into that and get better at other stuff?
turns.zh: 对于处于职业生涯中期或末期的设计师来说，你觉得他们是否需要精通技术、学会编程，或者至少能动手制作？还是说他们只需专注于其他领域也能成功？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I think it definitely helps to maybe not learn how to code so much that you're building something from scratch, but it does feel like more and more of the designer's vocabulary right now is implementing some stuff. I wonder though, as the models, both the models and the products get better, I mean, we probably will continue to move up the abstraction layers and you won't have to actually know how each single line of code will work. But I think what I would say is start to bring that into your toolkit, the coding tools, whether or not it's like you're actually becoming technical, I think any designer should just be really aware, and know how to use the tools that are at hand, as opposed to maybe learning and going off and learning React or et cetera, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我觉得不必非得精通编程才能从零开始创造，但现在设计师的核心技能确实越来越倾向于实现功能了。不过我觉得，随着模型和产品不断优化，我们很可能会向更高的抽象层迈进，不必深入理解每行代码的具体运作。但我要说的是，开始把编程工具纳入技能库吧——即便不成为技术专家，任何设计师都应该熟悉现有工具，知道如何高效使用，而不是去学习React之类的框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How good of a designer is Claude, would you say, or Claude Code, however you want to describe ... Would you hire Claude as a designer or is it not there yet?
turns.zh: 你觉得Claude作为设计师的水平如何？或者说Claude Code（无论你怎么称呼它）……你会聘用Claude做设计师吗？还是说它目前还不够成熟？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I don't think Claude is there yet. I don't think Claude is there yet in terms of a designer you would hire. I think it is not yet the strong generalist or the deep specialist or the crack new grad. I think it's pretty good at a first pass, and at presenting a bunch of different ideas to you, but nothing there quite feels like special and hireable yet.
turns.zh: 我觉得克劳德现在还达不到标准。就你会聘请的设计师而言，克劳德目前还不够格。我认为他既不是那种全能型人才，也不是那种专精某一领域的专家，更不是那种出色的应届生。他初稿做得还不错，能为你呈现不少不同的创意方案，但目前还没有那种令人惊艳、值得聘用的水准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is good news for designers for now. It sucks at this for now. And I'm so curious to see how good it could get at this. That's such a big open question, is can it pump out amazing novel, unique creative experiences, or it's just never going to be that good as a human designer?
turns.zh: 不过对设计师来说这倒是个好消息。目前他在这方面表现不佳。我特别好奇他能否在这方面有所突破。这是个悬而未决的大问题：它能否创造出令人惊叹的新奇、独特的创意体验，还是说永远无法超越人类设计师的水平？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: I mean, it's gotten a lot better in the last year or so, even. So yeah.
turns.zh: 说真的，过去一年左右它确实有了很大的进步。所以确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple management, I don't know, rituals or takes you have that I've heard from folks that you work with, that I want to touch on. One is that you have this hot take that low leverage time for managers is just not a thing, that there's a lot of benefit you can get out of things that people consider low leverage. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 还有一些管理方面的经验或策略，我从同事那里听说过，挺想跟你聊聊的。其中一个观点是，你认为管理者投入低效时间没什么意义，但其实从那些被认为低效的事情中也能收获不少价值。你能谈谈这个吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I remember first becoming a manager, and I think one of the pieces of advice that I either got from a course or a book or something, is like, yeah, "Now that you're a manager, you have to really prioritize your time and categorize your work." And there was this two by two of ... I don't remember what it was in it, but you essentially say, "Oh, these are the things that only I can do. These are things anybody else can do, and everything else, it's low leverage and you shouldn't do that anymore." And a lot of the low leverage things were just things that are really nitpicky in the weeds, or just literally, yes, probably somebody else could do those tasks. But when I think about leaders and managers that I respect the most, I actually think some of their best traits is that they choose low leverage tasks that they take on themselves, and that actually ends up being actually a very high leverage thing, because it's them who's doing it. (00:56:00): So one example is whenever you have senior leaders who just test the shit out of the product, and they're just so in tune with it, and they dog food it, they repro the bugs, they spend a bunch of time with engineers sharing the logs and nitpicking and stuff like that. And I think that ends up being super actually high leverage, even though it's a lot of time, of nitty-gritty time, because it creates this familiarity with the product, which I think is really good. It also creates this vibe where it's like, oh yeah, this senior leader really cares deeply and they actually know the ins and out of the product, and they're rolling up their sleeves and they're giving this feedback and working with the team on it. (00:56:39): And I think similarly to what I've seen is when a senior leader is able to fix a bug now. I think I've actually seen Mike Krieger before put in PRs himself, and it's really nice because it's like, okay, cool, we're all on this team together and nothing is below this person. And I think another thing that I love that's a little bit more cultural, is when somebody goes out of the way to make somebody's anniversary card or something, and vibe code them something super nice, or make them something, a super nice card, because I think it just shows that it's like an EA or somebody can put together the card, but this leader is just somebody who cares so much about their team that they put in the effort. So that's something I try to embody, is choosing the seemingly low leverage tasks that are worth my time.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊。我记得刚开始当经理的时候，我从某个课程或书籍中学到的一条建议是：“既然你现在是经理了，你就必须真正优先安排自己的时间，并对工作进行分类。”然后还有一个二维表格……我不记得具体内容了，但大意是：“哦，这些事只有我能做。这些事任何人都能做，其余的都是低效益的，你不应该再做了。” 很多低效益的事其实都是些细枝末节的小事，或者确实是别人能做的。但在我最尊敬的领导者和管理者身上，我发现他们最优秀的特质之一，就是会主动承担那些低效益的任务。结果这些任务反倒成了高效益的，因为只有他们自己才能做到这一点。

（00:56:00）：比如，当你看到那些高级领导对产品进行深度测试时，他们对产品了如指掌，自己使用产品，亲自调试漏洞，与工程师一起分析日志、挑剔细节等等。我认为这最终带来了极高的效益，虽然这需要大量细致入微的时间，但它能让他们对产品了如指掌，这真的很棒。还能营造出一种氛围，让人感觉这位高级领导真的很在乎产品，深入了解产品细节，亲自参与反馈并与团队合作。

（00:56:39）：类似的例子还有，当高级领导能亲自修复漏洞时。我记得曾见过Mike Krieger亲自提交PR（代码提交请求），这真的很棒，因为这传递出一种信号：好吧，很酷，我们都是团队的一员，没有什么事是低人一等的。还有一点让我很感动的是，当有人特意为别人制作周年卡片，或者用心准备礼物时，我觉得这恰恰说明，虽然EA（工程师助理）可以帮忙制作卡片，但这位领导真正在乎团队，才会亲自下功夫。这也是我努力效仿的——选择那些看似低效益却值得我投入时间的任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that is so interesting. What you're saying there is, in a sense, the low leverage stuff is the stuff that often has the most impact because your reports wouldn't expect you to spend time on this thing, and the low leverage ends up being high leverage.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太有意思了。你说的意思是，从某种角度来说，低效益的工作往往能产生最大的影响，因为下属不会期望你花时间在这些事情上，而低效益的工作最终却成了高效益的工作。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. And I think it's what makes your style of leadership stand out, or feel special to a certain person.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这正是你的领导风格之所以与众不同，或者对某些人来说特别之处所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Another, I don't know, ritual and way of running teams that I heard about you, is you encourage team members roasting each other, which on the surface doesn't sound like a wonderful environment, but on the other hand, I hear constantly that the teams that you've built are just the happiest, the highest performing teams. Talk about, I guess, this idea of roasting and encouraging that, and just what you've learned about building awesome teams.
turns.zh: 太棒了。另外，我不知道，你提到的另一个仪式和管理团队的方式，是鼓励团队成员互相调侃。虽然表面上这听起来不是一个理想的工作环境，但另一方面，我经常听说你组建的团队是最快乐、表现最出色的团队。能不能谈谈这种互相调侃和鼓励的理念，以及你对组建优秀团队的见解？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's not that I'm like, "Yo, you should roast each other." I'm not forcing it in that way or anything, but when I think about the psychological safety, and teams and people that just get along with each other, when you think about your friends, you're always willing to push the boundaries a little bit and roast them. You're roasting your friends a lot, but you actually might not be roasting your coworkers a lot, because it's all just about comfort and safety. So it's not that I'm like, "Oh, I want my teams to roast each other." But I think it can be a really good sign when the people on your team feel comfortable just poking fun at each other a little bit. And I think that also can be a good sign when folks also feel the same way about you as a leader, where it's like there's just an element of they don't fear you as much, and they feel like there's a sense of safety where if they say something, they're not going to get fired. (00:59:14): So an example of this is, with my last team, I feel like they would make fun of things that I would say at crits sometimes, certain phrases I would say.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这不是说我会去说：“嘿，你们应该互相吐槽一下。”我不是刻意逼迫大家这么做，但当我考虑心理安全感、团队合作以及人们相处融洽的时候——想想你的朋友们，你总是愿意稍微突破一下界限去调侃他们。你经常拿朋友开玩笑，但对同事可能就不会这么频繁了，因为这关乎舒适感和安全感。所以我不是说我希望团队成员互相吐槽，但当团队成员能自在地互相调侃时，这确实是个很好的信号。同样，当下属对你作为领导者也有同样的感觉——他们不再那么畏惧你，感到有安全感，只要说出自己的想法就不会被解雇，这也是个积极的信号。（00:59:14）：举个例子，我上一支团队有时会在评审会上拿我说笑，调侃我某些特定的表达方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Oh, I would always be like, "Okay, what are next steps, and how do we follow up on this?" And then they'd be like, "Okay, what are next steps?" And they would sort of channel me in that way. Yeah, I just think it shows a level of like, okay, these people are not necessarily afraid of me, they know that they trust me, they can trust me, and then they sort of know enough about each other, and me personally and our personal lives, to be able to know where those boundaries are. But at the same time, I think the thing that you err into in that territory, is as a manager, are you friends with your reports? Which is I think a thing people tell you not to do. And so the way I think about balancing this out is you have to create this baseline of psychological safety, and people feel comfortable both with each other and with you, but you also have to make sure that they know that you have really high standards. (01:00:24): And I think these two things can feel like they're at tension, but I think they work really well together, because it's like once you have that psychological safety, you have people trusting each other and you, applying the high standards actually I think becomes potentially easier because you can do it without fear, I think. And I sort of think about this from the approach of being a tough parent a little bit. It's like, "Oh yeah, my team, I work with them in a way where they know I'm always going to be there and I'm not just going to fire them on a whim or something. But at the same time, they also know that I want the best for them, and that I have high standards, and that I'm working with them to make the best work possible." And so yeah, that's the balance I think you just strike is like, can you create this environment of one where your team feels comfortable roasting you, but at the same time they know they have to be doing great work, and they will do great work with you.
turns.zh: 哦，我总是会说：“好的，下一步该做什么？怎么跟进？”然后他们也会说：“好的，下一步该做什么？” 他们会模仿我的说话方式。是啊，我觉得这表明大家不害怕我，他们信任我，知道我会公正对待他们，而且团队成员之间、包括他们和我个人，甚至我们的私生活都足够了解，知道彼此的底线在哪里。但与此同时，作为管理者，你可能会陷入一个误区——和下属成为朋友？我觉得这是个被告诫不要做的行为。所以我认为平衡这两者的关键在于，首先要建立心理安全感，让团队成员既能自在地互相调侃，也能信任你，但同时你也要确保他们知道你有很高的标准。（01:00:24）：我觉得这两者看似矛盾，但其实能很好地协同。有了心理安全感后，大家就会信任彼此和信任你，执行高标准也会变得更容易，因为人们不会心怀恐惧地去做事。说到这，我有点把自己当成严厉家长的感觉。比如：“是啊，我的团队，我和他们合作的方式是，他们知道我会一直在，绝不会随意解雇他们。但同时他们也知道我希望他们做到最好，我有高标准，会和他们一起努力创造出最出色的工作成果。” 所以我认为关键在于，你要营造一个环境，让团队成员既能自在地调侃你，又知道必须出色完成工作，这样他们才会和你一起出色完成任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is awesome advice. It's interesting how often this just management style comes back, or management, good management, it comes back, reminds me of, what was it, radical candor, just this combination of caring deeply and challenging directly. And that's kind of what I hear here, is just make sure people know that you care deeply about them, but also be very direct and have high standards.
turns.zh: 真是很棒的建议。有趣的是，这种管理风格经常被提起，或者说管理层、优秀的管理方式都会被反复提及。这让我想起什么来着？是"彻底坦诚"（Radical Candor）吗？就是那种既深切关怀又直言不讳的管理方式。听起来这里的核心理念就是，要让员工知道你真心在乎他们，同时也要保持直言不讳，树立高标准。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. Okay. Maybe a final question. I'm always looking for interesting frameworks and methods and processes that people have found useful in their work. And I hear you're a big fan of something called the legibility framework. Talk about this, talk about how you use it, why it's so valuable.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。好吧，最后再问个问题。我一直在寻找人们在工作中觉得有用的框架、方法和流程。我听说你特别推崇一个叫做"可读性框架"的东西。能讲讲这个框架吗？讲讲你是如何运用它的，以及它为何如此有价值。

turns.speaker: Jenny Wen
turns.en: Yeah. This framework, I think I saw it on Twitter, maybe last year or something, and it was Evan Tana, who's a partner at SPC. He's a VC. So it basically is this two by two. I don't think it got so much attention, but once I started seeing it, I actually couldn't stop thinking about it. So on the two by two, he basically has founders. Founders can be either illegible or legible, and then ideas can either be illegible or legible. And basically he was saying that, "Okay, if both the founder and idea is super legible, the idea is probably not that novel, and somebody's already like, they're already going to implement it or do it and you're actually not finding something new." But then where it gets really interesting is where the idea itself is illegible. And by illegible, he means, "Oh, it's sort of really on the frontier, people might not get it yet," or the way it's being told, it's not being told in the way that makes the most sense to people. (01:03:06): And I think this is obviously a good way for a VC to operate, because you're trying to look for the opportunities that people don't see and put them out there in the world. But I also think that part of the role of the designer, at least, at least at a frontier lab at Anthropic, is spotting the ideas that are illegible, and trying to understand what's there, and how to take that and transform it, whether it's through storytelling, or whether it's through the actual UX and the form factor, and put it out there. And I think when I mentioned going through Slack and looking at all the stuff that people are making, that's kind of what I'm doing. I'm trying to see, oh yeah, what are the ideas that there's some energy there around, but might not make sense yet, that are worth me thinking about more in my work? (01:03:57): There's one good example, actually, that ties to cowork where there was this internal prototype that we called Claude Studio that I think somebody built partway through last year, and it essentially was just this really kind of dense, powerful interface that was built on top of some agentic harness. It might've been Claude Code at that point in time too. And it had all these displays where it was showing you all this knowledge and all these skills and things Claude was doing, and previewing its outputs. And I think, to a designer, I looked at it and I was like, "I don't know what's going on. I don't really get it." But then I sort of saw the folks in research, the folks building it and just folks internally, there's just a lot of energy around it. And I was like, "Cool, I think there's something here, but I just don't understand it yet." And I think that really was an example of an illegible idea. (01:04:56): And ultimately what came from it was the skills framework and the markdown files that instruct Claude on how to do something. So that came out of that specific prototype. That was not something I was directly involved in, and that was more of, the folks working this prototype extracted that out of it. But when it did come to work on Claude cowork and I was thinking about, oh yeah, what is the form factor for those things? Seeing that prototype and seeing the kinds of information that people found really helpful, seeing Claude's plan and to-dos, seeing Claude's context and the files that it was going through, those kinds of things are things that I ended up pulling out of that prototype into Claude cowork. So yeah, I think about how can designers almost be more like VCs in this way, internally when we're looking at prototypes.
turns.zh:
是啊。我记得这个框架，我在推特上看到过，可能是在去年之类的，发帖人是SPC的合伙人埃文·塔纳（Evan Tana），他是一位风险投资家。这个框架本质上是一个二维矩阵。我觉得它当时没引起太多关注，但我一看到它，就一直思考这个模型。矩阵分为两行两列：创始人要么清晰明了，要么晦涩难懂；创意要么清晰明了，要么晦涩难懂。塔纳的核心观点是，如果创始人和创意都非常清晰，那这个创意可能就没什么新意了，因为别人可能已经在实施了。但真正有趣的地方在于，当创意本身也很晦涩时。比如创意可能处于前沿领域，人们可能还不太理解，或者表达方式不够清晰。

（01:03:06）我认为这对风险投资家来说是个很好的策略，因为他们要寻找别人看不到的机会，并将其推向市场。但我也认为设计师的角色，至少在Anthropic的前沿实验室里，就是发现那些晦涩的创意，试图理解其本质，并通过讲故事、用户体验设计或产品形态，将其转化为可行的方案。正如我之前提到的，我会浏览Slack上的所有项目，试图发现那些尚未被完全理解但充满潜力的创意，值得我在工作中深入思考。

（01:03:57）有一个很好的例子，和Cowork相关。我们有一个内部原型叫Claude Studio，去年年底有人部分完成。它本质上是一个基于某种智能代理框架（当时可能是Claude Code）的密集且强大的界面，有多个显示屏展示Claude的知识、技能和输出预览。作为设计师，我看完后觉得一头雾水，但看到研发团队和内部人员对它充满热情时，我意识到“这里面肯定有潜力，只是目前我还不明白”。这正是那个晦涩创意的典型例子。

（01:04:56）最终，这个原型催生了技能框架和Markdown文件，用于指导Claude的操作流程。这是从那个原型中提取出来的。我没有直接参与其中，但团队从原型中提取了这些内容。后来，当我参与Cowork项目时，我会思考这些产品的形态。比如看到原型中人们觉得很有用的信息展示，Claude的计划和待办事项，背景信息和文件处理方式等，这些都被我整合到了Cowork项目中。是啊，我觉得设计师在内部审视原型时，应该更像风险投资家那样，善于发现潜力。

turns.en: This is super interesting. You're never going to do this. This is the craziest thing. Why would you even think ... " OpenAI actually was one of them, just some research lab doing some stuff. So it's interesting that ... And it's not like every time this will work, and it's not like every crazy idea that makes no sense will be good. But I think what you're saying is pay attention to stuff that's interesting to you and isn't totally clear. Maybe you can be the person that helps pull it together.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.en: Yeah. Because I think people who often gravitate towards these early ideas, they can't always articulate why. And it's sort of up to you to dive deeper and understand that.
